oneSentence: Calibration describes how closely a system’s probability scores match the observed frequencies of the corresponding outcomes.
plainExplanation:
Many AI systems do not just give a label such as “spam” or “not spam”. They may also give a probability score, such as 0.8 for “spam”. Calibration asks a simple question: among many similar cases scored around 0.8 for spam, are about 80% actually spam?

What goes in is a set of predictions with probability scores and the true outcomes. What happens is that we group predictions with similar scores, then compare the average score with what really happened. What comes out is a picture or summary of whether the scores match observed outcome frequencies.

A system can have good accuracy and still be badly calibrated. For example, it might rank risky cases above safer ones correctly, but assign probabilities that are far too high. That matters because people often use the score itself to choose a threshold, assign attention, or judge uncertainty.

Calibration is often confused with probability itself. A model output may assign estimated likelihood to each option. Calibration tests whether those numbers match observed frequencies. Calibration is also different from precision and recall, which focus on classification results after a threshold is chosen, not on whether probability scores match reality.

everydayAnalogy.title: Journey times on a city travel board
everydayAnalogy.story:
At a large bus station, an electronic board predicts the chance that each bus will arrive within 10 minutes. For many buses, the board says “70% chance”. Over the next month, staff check all the cases where it said 70%. If roughly 7 out of 10 of those buses really do arrive within 10 minutes, that confidence level is well calibrated.

If only 4 out of 10 arrive in time, the board was too confident. If 9 out of 10 arrive in time, it was too cautious.

mapping.analogyElement: staff checking many past buses with the same message
how often buses actually arrived within 10 minutes
mapping.aiElement: the observed frequency of correct outcomes

mapping.analogyElement: too confident or too cautious travel estimates

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A travel board predicts one event in the world, while many AI systems score categories, risks or rankings. Also, calibration is checked across groups of similar predictions, not by asking whether one single 70% prediction was 'right'. A perfectly calibrated system can still be unhelpful if it separates cases poorly, and the bus example does not show that distinction clearly.

visual.title: High accuracy, poor calibration versus good calibration
visual.learningObjective: Show that confidence scores can be useful only if they match observed frequencies, not merely if many predictions are correct.
visual.description: Two side-by-side columns compare systems on the same 100 cases. Each column shows score bands from low to high confidence and the observed share correct in each band. Read top to bottom within a column, then compare columns: one system is accurate but overconfident, the other has scores that line up with reality.

steps.label: Same task, same cases
steps.explanation: Both systems predict the same yes-or-no task on the same test set of 100 cases.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw two equal panels labelled System A and System B. Above both, place a shared caption: 'Same 100 test cases'. Use identical layout in both panels.

steps.label: System A gives high scores
steps.explanation: System A often outputs 0.9 confidence, but among those cases it is correct only about 0.7 of the time.
steps.visualInstruction: In System A, draw three horizontal score bands: 0.3, 0.6, 0.9. Next to each, show an observed correct rate bar. Make the 0.9 score band align with a 0.7 observed bar, using contrasting colours and a small label 'too confident'.

steps.label: System B lines up better
steps.explanation: System B’s score bands are close to the observed frequencies, so its numbers behave more like usable probabilities.
steps.visualInstruction: In System B, draw the same three score bands. Align 0.3 with about 0.3 observed, 0.6 with about 0.6, and 0.9 with about 0.9. Add a label 'well calibrated'.

steps.label: Why the difference matters
steps.explanation: If a person acts only on cases above 0.8, System A may create misplaced trust, even if its overall accuracy looks similar.
steps.visualInstruction: Below both panels, add a threshold line at 0.8 and a short note: 'Thresholds and risk decisions rely on trustworthy confidence scores'.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each score band to reveal a short tooltip: 'Predicted confidence' and 'Observed share correct'.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram compares two systems on the same 100 cases. In both, predictions are grouped into confidence bands such as 0.3, 0.6 and 0.9. In System A, the 0.9 band is correct only about 70% of the time, so the scores are too high for reality. In System B, each confidence band closely matches the observed share correct, so the scores are well calibrated. The main point is that two systems can look similar on overall performance, yet only one gives confidence numbers that behave like probabilities.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static side-by-side chart shows System A with mismatched score bands and observed outcomes, and System B with closely matched bands and outcomes. Text labels explain 'too confident' and 'well calibrated' without animation.

workedExample.scenario: For an illustrative validation exercise, the translation service compares the tool's scores with completed human screening of 100 applications for a rostered profile.
workedExample.input: One hundred previously screened applications, with the model score and confirmed screening outcome for each.
process: Group the applications by score: 20 near 0.2, 30 near 0.5 and 50 near 0.8.
Calculate the share in each group that human screening confirmed as meeting the profile.
In the 0.2 group, 4 of 20 met the profile, corresponding to 20%.
In the 0.5 group, 15 of 30 met the profile, corresponding to 50%.
In the 0.8 group, 30 of 50 met the profile, corresponding to 60%, not 80%.
workedExample.result: In this illustrative sample, the lower two score groups are calibrated, while the tool is overconfident in the 0.8 group. It may still rank stronger applications above weaker ones, but staff cannot interpret 0.8 as an 80% likelihood without recalibration or further validation.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: At a duty station with three working languages, a reviser in the translation service checks a pilot tool that scores how likely each application is to meet a rostered translator profile. The long list and screening sheet are due to the selection panel at close of business.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Calibration shows whether applications given, for example, a 0.8 score are later confirmed as meeting the profile about 80% of the time. The reviser should also check calibration by working language, since acceptable overall results can conceal uneven reliability between groups.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Applications contain personal and HR-sensitive material. They must not be entered into any tool not approved for that material. Minimise the data used, restrict access and retain human review. A probability score must not become an automatic ground for excluding an applicant.

whyItMatters:
Confidence scores often shape action. A manager may prioritise cases above 0.9, a reviewer may skip checks below 0.2, or a rights-focused team may escalate cases marked high risk. If those scores are not calibrated, people can trust the wrong cases too much or discount important ones.

This matters especially where harms are uneven. Overconfident scores can hide uncertainty in cases affecting access to services, moderation, fraud checks, or risk screening. A system may look strong on a headline metric while still giving misleading confidence. For non-specialists, calibration is a practical question: 'When this system sounds sure, how often is that justified?'
whereYouMayHearIt: A translation service review before a roster-screening pilot is cleared
A vendor demo during a procurement meeting
An evaluation office discussion of a reliability diagram
An ICT governance board review of whether probability scores are fit for use

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If a model is accurate, its confidence scores must already be trustworthy.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Accuracy counts how many predictions are right overall. Calibration checks whether the stated confidence matches reality. A model can be accurate because it usually picks the right label, yet still give 95% confidence in cases where it is right only 70% of the time.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A 70% score tells you what will happen in this single case.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Calibration is about long-run frequency across many similar cases, not certainty about one case. A well-calibrated 70% score means that among many cases given about 70%, roughly 70% turn out correct.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Calibration only matters for highly technical users.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Anyone using thresholds, triage rules or risk bands is relying on confidence scores. If the scores are miscalibrated, operational choices can be distorted even when the interface looks simple.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: A system is well calibrated when its probability scores match what happens over time. If it assigns 80% to an outcome in many cases, that outcome should occur about 80% of the time.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: For probabilistic predictions, calibration means agreement between predicted probabilities and empirical outcome frequencies. In binary classification, if we collect instances assigned score p, the event should occur about p of the time within that group. It is often examined with reliability diagrams, calibration curves, or summary measures such as calibration error, though the exact metric and binning method vary. Calibration differs from discrimination or ranking quality: a model can order cases well yet be systematically overconfident or underconfident. It can also be improved after training by recalibration methods, but recalibration itself must be validated on appropriate data to avoid leakage or overfitting.

keyTakeaway: Calibration asks whether stated probabilities match observed frequencies. It is not the same as ranking accuracy: a model may order cases well while giving misleading confidence scores.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best describes a well-calibrated classifier?
options: Its confidence scores match how often it is correct across many similar cases.
It always gives high confidence for correct predictions and low confidence for wrong ones.
It has the highest possible accuracy on the test set.
quickCheck.explanation: Calibration compares probability or confidence scores with observed frequencies. Ranking cases well, using equal-sized groups, or producing high confidence does not show that the score values match outcomes.

issues.problem: The page alternates between two different meanings of a score. It sometimes defines calibration as confidence matching the frequency of the model being correct, but the worked example tests whether a score for the outcome “routine” matches the frequency of that outcome. These are not interchangeable. For a routine score of 0.2, 20% routine means the outcome probability is calibrated, while the predicted label may be correct 80% of the time.
issues.fix: Define calibration in terms of probability scores and their corresponding outcomes. When specifically discussing confidence in a selected label, say that the relevant outcome is whether that label is correct.

issues.problem: The board predicts whether an event will occur, but the mapping calls occurrence a “correct outcome”. A single probabilistic forecast is not evaluated as correct merely because the event occurs, or incorrect merely because it does not. Calibration concerns frequencies over repeated forecasts.
issues.fix: Map bus arrivals to “the observed frequency of the predicted event”. State that one forecast cannot establish calibration because calibration compares scores with frequencies across many cases.

issues.problem: The claim that confidence scores “can be useful only if” they are calibrated is false. Miscalibrated scores can still be useful for ranking or discrimination, even though their numerical values should not be treated as reliable probabilities.
issues.fix: Show that confidence scores should match observed frequencies before their numerical values are treated as probabilities, even if many predictions are correct.

issues.problem: The visual mixes positive-outcome probabilities with confidence in correctness. On a yes-or-no task, 0.3 can be a probability for “yes”, but then it must be compared with the observed share of yes outcomes, not the share correct. If the number is confidence in the selected label, binary confidence would normally be at least 0.5. The visual also calls System A highly accurate and says the systems have similar overall performance without providing band counts or enough outcomes to establish either claim.
issues.fix: Retitle it “Poor calibration versus good calibration”. Treat every score as the predicted probability of “yes” and compare it with the observed share of yes outcomes. Remove the claims that System A is highly accurate and that overall performance is similar unless the visual supplies counts that demonstrate those claims.

issues.problem: The arithmetic itself is correct: 20 + 30 + 50 = 100, 4/20 = 0.20, 15/30 = 0.50, and 30/50 = 0.60. However, the groups are described as being “near” 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8. Without each group’s average predicted score, the page cannot say that 20% and 50% match the predictions exactly.
issues.fix: Change the first process step to: “Group the 100 messages by model score: 20 scored 0.2, 30 scored 0.5, and 50 scored 0.8.” Qualify the result as applying to this sample.

issues.problem: These fields repeat the same conflation between the probability of an outcome and confidence that the selected label is correct. That directly conflicts with the worked example, which evaluates the frequency of the outcome “routine”.
issues.fix: Describe an 80% score as matching an outcome frequency. A selected-label confidence score can instead be compared with how often that selected label is correct.

issues.problem: The marked option is the intended definition, but the alternatives do not provide a sound test. Option 1 can also describe a calibrated classifier, depending on what “high” and “low” mean. Options 2 and 3 use obvious absolutes and can be rejected without understanding calibration.
issues.fix: Keep option 0. Replace the other options with: “Its scores put cases in the right order, even when their values do not match outcomes.”; “Each confidence band contains the same number of cases.”; “Its average confidence is as high as possible on the test set.” Update the explanation to distinguish calibration from ranking, bin sizes and high confidence.
